questions.prompt: Which reason for using a tuple does the note give?
options: It lets a method return multiple values without creating a class or struct
It is the only way to store values of different types together
It makes its elements dynamically typed
It replaces the need for collections like `List<T>`
questions.explanation: A tuple groups multiple values so a method can return them without defining a separate class or struct, and it reads better than `out`/`ref` parameters while staying strongly typed.

questions.prompt: What does the C# 7.0+ syntax `var person = (Id: 1, Name: "Aman");` offer over `new Tuple<int, string>(1, "Aman")`?
options: It allows more than eight elements without nesting
It turns the tuple into a class you can inherit from
Named elements such as `person.Id` and `person.Name` instead of `.Item1` and `.Item2`
It stops the elements from being strongly typed
questions.explanation: Old-style tuples are accessed with `.Item1`, `.Item2` and so on; modern tuples can be declared with names and accessed as named properties like `.Id` and `.Name`.
The third element is itself a tuple `(85, "Math")`, so `nestedTuple.Item3.Item1` is 85 and `nestedTuple.Item3.Item2` is `Math`.

questions.prompt: What does the note say about storing more than 7 values in a tuple?
options: It is impossible; tuples hold at most 7 values
Every value after the seventh is silently dropped
Tuples have a direct capacity of 8 elements, so the 8th element must itself be a nested tuple
questions.explanation: Tuples have a maximum direct capacity of 8 elements; to store more than 7 values, the 8th element must be a nested tuple.
